---
title: "Bloaters: When Code Grows Too Big to Hold in Your Head"
---

## The core idea

No one *writes* a bloater on purpose. Bloaters build up over time. Each change adds "just one more parameter" or "just one more `if`," and each step is reasonable on its own. The trouble is in the economics: at each moment, **adding is cheaper than restructuring**, so code grows instead of being reorganized. It's the boiling-frog problem.

The real cost of a bloater is **cognitive load**, not size. Human working memory holds about 4–7 items. When a unit of code asks you to track more than that, you start making mistakes.

The four bloaters often travel together and feed one another:

```
   Data Clumps ──────► Long Parameter List ──────► Long Function ──────► Large Class
  (data that belongs   (the clumps get passed      (with many inputs,     (long functions
   together but isn't   around as loose args)       functions do many      pile up in one
   grouped)                                         things)                class)

        └──────────────── root cause: missing abstractions ────────────────┘
```

So we'll use **one running example** that has all four smells and fix it step by step.

---

## The smelly starting point

```python
def generate_report(patient_name, patient_hn, patient_age,
                    study_date, modality, body_part,
                    findings, radiologist, is_urgent, lang):
    # --- validate ---
    if not patient_hn or len(patient_hn) != 7:
        raise ValueError("Invalid HN")
    if modality not in ("CT", "MR", "US", "CR"):
        raise ValueError("Unknown modality")
    # --- header ---
    header = f"{patient_name}  HN: {patient_hn}  Age: {patient_age}\n"
    header += f"{modality} {body_part}  ({study_date})\n"
    # --- findings ---
    body = "".join(f"- {f}\n" for f in findings)
    # --- urgency ---
    if is_urgent:
        header = "*** URGENT ***\n" + header
    # --- language ---
    title = "รายงานผลการตรวจ" if lang == "th" else "Radiology Report"
    return f"{title}\n{header}\n{body}\nReported by: {radiologist}"
```

It works, and it's only about 20 lines. Now imagine it a year later, after 15 more features have been added. Here's what's already wrong with it.

---

## 1. Data Clumps: find the missing nouns

**Symptom:** The same group of data items always shows up together. Here there are two clumps:

```
patient_name, patient_hn, patient_age   ← always travel together
study_date, modality, body_part         ← always travel together
```

**Fowler's test:** Delete one item from the group. Do the others still make sense on their own? A `patient_age` without a patient is meaningless, so this is a clump that should become an object.

**Cure:** Extract Class / Introduce Parameter Object.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Patient:
    name: str
    hn: str
    age: int

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Study:
    date: str
    modality: str
    body_part: str
```

**The deeper payoff:** A clump is a *concept from your domain that hasn't been named yet*. Once it has a name, **behavior starts to move into it**. HN validation clearly belongs to `Patient`, not to the report generator:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Patient:
    name: str
    hn: str
    age: int

    def __post_init__(self):
        if len(self.hn) != 7:
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid HN: {self.hn}")
```

Now an invalid `Patient` *cannot exist*, so no other function ever needs to re-check it. This is the most important lesson in the Bloaters family: **naming a concept moves knowledge to the place where it belongs.**

---

## 2. Long Parameter List: count what the caller must know

**Symptom:** Our signature has 10 parameters. Every caller has to know all ten, get their order right, and change whenever one is added.

**Cures**, three of which apply here:

| Refactoring | Applied here |
|---|---|
| **Introduce Parameter Object** | 6 loose args become `patient, study` |
| **Remove Flag Argument** | `is_urgent` is a boolean that *switches behavior*, and `True` at the call site tells the reader nothing |
| **Preserve Whole Object** | Pass `patient`, not `patient.name, patient.hn` |

A flag argument is a hidden second function. Compare the call sites:

```python
generate_report(p, s, f, r, True, "th")   # True what? "th" why?
generate_urgent_report(p, s, f, r)         # intent is visible
```

**Rule of thumb:** Parameters should be things the function *operates on*, not settings that *pick which function to be*.

---

## 3. Long Function: comments are seams

**Symptom:** Look at the comments, `# --- validate ---`, `# --- header ---`, and so on. Each one is the author admitting, *"this block has a purpose I couldn't express in code."*

Fowler's heuristic:

> Whenever you feel the need to comment a block, write a function instead, and name it after the comment's **intent**.

**Cure:** Extract Function, using each comment as a cut line:

```python
def generate_report(patient: Patient, study: Study,
                    findings: list[str], radiologist: str) -> str:
    return "\n".join([
        render_header(patient, study),
        render_findings(findings),
        render_signature(radiologist),
    ])
```

Now the function reads like a table of contents. You see **what** happens at one level of abstraction, and you go into a helper only when you need the **how**.

An important point: Fowler says length is a poor measure. What matters is the **semantic distance between the function's name and its body**. A 3-line function that mixes SQL, formatting, and business rules is "long." A 30-line function that does one clear thing at one level of abstraction may be fine.

```
  Good function                          Bloated function
  ─────────────                          ────────────────
  name:  render_header                   name:  generate_report
  body:  one level of detail             body:  validation + formatting +
         ↓ (short gap)                          i18n + business rules
         "I can see the name                    ↓ (huge gap)
          in the body"                          "the name hides 5 jobs"
```

---

## 4. Large Class: the function's home becomes the next bloater

Suppose `generate_report` lives in a class that has grown over time:

```
ReportService
├── fetch_from_pacs()          ┐
├── pacs_host, pacs_port       ┘ ← PACS integration
├── validate_hn()              ┐
├── validate_modality()        ┘ ← domain rules
├── render_header()            ┐
├── render_findings()          │ ← formatting
├── translate()                ┘
├── send_email()               ┐
└── smtp_server                ┘ ← notification
```

**Fowler's detection trick:** Look for **subsets of fields and methods that are used together**, and for **shared prefixes and suffixes** in names (`pacs_*`, `smtp_*`, `render_*`). Each cluster is a class waiting to be extracted.

**Cure:** Extract Class (and sometimes Extract Superclass).

```
         BEFORE                                AFTER
  ┌──────────────────┐            ┌─────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │  ReportService   │            │ PacsClient  │   │ ReportRender │
  │ (4 reasons to    │    ──►     └─────────────┘   └──────────────┘
  │  change)         │            ┌─────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  └──────────────────┘            │  Patient    │   │  Notifier    │
                                  │ (rules)     │   └──────────────┘
                                  └─────────────┘
```

This is the **Single Responsibility Principle** seen from the opposite side. SRP tells you how to *design*, and the Large Class smell tells you how to *detect* a violation in existing code.

---

## The whole picture

```
 SMELL                 QUESTION TO ASK                       MAIN CURE
 ───────────────────   ───────────────────────────────────   ──────────────────────
 Data Clumps           "What concept am I failing to name?"  Extract Class
 Long Parameter List   "What must the caller know?"          Parameter Object,
                                                             Remove Flag Argument
 Long Function         "Where are the comment-seams?"        Extract Function
 Large Class           "Which fields/methods cluster?"       Extract Class
```

## A warning about over-correcting

Every cure can be overdone. If you extract too much, you get a different family of smells: **Lazy Element** (classes too small to justify themselves) and **Middle Man** (layers that only delegate). The goal is not "small." The goal is that **each unit can be understood on its own**. We'll see this tension in the Dispensables and Couplers lessons.
